title: Contract-manufacturing sourcing broker for CNC machining & sheet-metal parts (Midwest job-shop network)
product_service: Build-to-print custom parts and small assemblies (CNC machined, laser/sheet metal, weldments, with outside finishing) sourced from vetted independent job shops. Broker quotes, takes the PO and title, manages the supplier, inspects, and delivers.
target_customer: Design/manufacturing engineers and buyers at small-to-mid OEMs, machine builders, R&D labs and hardware startups (10-500 employees) needing prototypes and low-volume production. Illinois alone has 4,371 manufacturing establishments with 20+ employees [C, WS03-S006].
purchase_motivation: Speed and one point of contact; shortage of vetted shop capacity; avoiding supplier vetting; DFM help; domestic/USMCA sourcing to manage 2025-26 tariffs.
spending_evidence: Xometry marketplace revenue $629.6M in FY2025 from 81,821 active buyers (~$7.7k marketplace revenue per buyer, analyst calc) [B, WS03-S001]; Protolabs network (outsourced) revenue $116.2M, +15.7% [B, WS03-S002]; US machine shops shipped $44.7B in 2022 [C, WS03-S007].
representative_operators: Xometry - $686.6M revenue FY2025, marketplace GM 34.7%, still GAAP loss-making (net loss $61.7M) [B, WS03-S001]
Protolabs network segment - $116.2M FY2025 [B, WS03-S002]
Fictiv - ~250 partner factories, sold to MISUMI for $350M in 2025 after three loss years [C, WS03-S004; D, WS03-S005]
Independent human-led sourcing brokers - count and economics MISSING [E]
revenue_mechanism: Markup on supplier cost: customer price minus supplier price, finishing and freight. Incumbent platform realizes 34.7% marketplace gross margin [B, WS03-S001]; a new entrant competing on price is assumed 15-30% [E].
typical_transaction_value: $500-$15,000 per prototype PO; approved production programs $5k-$100k+/yr per part family [E]
direct_costs: Supplier part cost, outside processing (plating, heat treat, anodize), freight, inspection labor, rework/remake credits, card fees.
contribution_profit_note: Example: $5,000 PO at 22% gross margin = ~$1,100 gross profit before founder time and overhead [E]. Platform benchmark: $218.3M marketplace gross profit / 81,821 buyers = ~$2.7k gross profit per active buyer per year [B-derived, WS03-S001].
working_capital_note: Customers (OEMs) commonly pay net-30 to net-60; new suppliers may require prepayment or net-30. The broker can be funding 30-60 days of COGS, roughly 10-20% of annual revenue at scale [E]. Remakes after quality escapes are absorbed by the broker.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks from first RFQ to prototype PO; 3-12 months to win production programs (first-article, supplier approval).
repeat_purchase: recurring-programs: approved production parts reorder; prototypes episodic
acquisition_channels: Direct outreach to engineering/purchasing at Midwest OEMs identified via CBP/NAICS and directories
SEO RFQ landing pages by process/material
Referrals from job shops turning away out-of-scope work
Industrial trade shows and local manufacturing associations
customer_accessibility: Buyers are identifiable and reachable by B2B outreach. Many already use instant-quote platforms or trusted shops. Switching is easy for prototypes and slow for production parts.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed, not confirmed. Illinois has 829 machine shops and 182 sheet-metal shops [C, WS03-S006], and many are small (SUSB: 9,786 US machine-shop firms under $1M receipts [C, WS03-S008]) and lack sales staff. Xometry's 4,996 active suppliers show shops accept intermediaries [B, WS03-S001]. Willingness to quote a new broker reliably is unverified.
competitive_intensity: high - Xometry, Protolabs network, Fictiv/MISUMI, Chinese platforms, plus direct relationships with shops
entry_strategy: A human, engineer-led service for work that instant-quote engines handle poorly: complex tight-tolerance or multi-process parts, kitted assemblies, and drawings needing DFM. Offer a site-audited Chicago/Rockford supply base and documented domestic/USMCA origin for buyers who are tariff- or ITAR-sensitive. Quote within 24 hours.
licenses: Illinois business registration and IDOR sales-tax registration/resale certificates; general and product liability insurance; ITAR (DDTC) registration only if handling defense articles, which should be avoided initially [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low. Quality-system expectations (ISO 9001/AS9100) for aerospace and medical buyers; export controls (ITAR/EAR) for defense-related drawings.
operational_risks: Supplier late deliveries and quality escapes for which the broker is liable; disintermediation (customer goes direct to the shop); drawing confidentiality; founder quoting errors.
financial_risks: Receivables concentration with a few OEMs; funding remakes; supplier prepayment for new accounts.
geographic_constraints: Customers can be nationwide. Supplier audits favor a local supply base, and Chicago metro + Rockford hold most Illinois machine shops (Cook 222, DuPage 116, Winnebago 90) [C, WS03-S006].
founder_expertise: Blueprint/GD&T reading, machining and fabrication process knowledge, cost estimating, supplier auditing, first-article inspection basics.
staffing: Solo in year 1. Year 2: a quoting/project manager and a QC inspector (market wages, roughly $55-80k each [E]). Later: account managers, each owning a book of buyers.
automation_potential: AI and software can parse drawings, package RFQs, match suppliers, compare quotes, chase follow-ups and draft DFM notes. Supplier relationships, negotiation, quality judgement and dispute handling stay human.
delegation_potential: Medium. Account-manager and buyer roles exist in the labor market. Early supplier trust is tied to the founder.
scalability: Scales with account managers and supplier depth. Each account manager may carry roughly $250-500k gross profit per year at maturity [E]. More processes can be added (molding, castings).
expansion: Add injection molding (WS03-003) and reverse engineering (WS03-030). Then vertically integrate inspection, finishing (WS03-028) or a small CNC cell (WS03-026) only for proven repeat parts. Add private-label standard components.
roic_note: Capital at risk is mainly working capital ($10-50k) plus small tooling and insurance. If receivables are controlled, operating profit / capital can exceed 200% [E].
critical_assumptions: A new broker can win RFQs against instant-quote platforms at 15-30% markup
Local shops will quote reliably and hold quality for a broker
Buyers accept a broker without ISO 9001 initially
unanswered_questions: Realized markups of small independent brokers
Share of Illinois shops willing to work through a broker
Typical supplier payment terms for a new broker
failure_modes: One quality escape loses a key account
Customers or suppliers cut out the broker
Founder remains the only salesperson and quoter

title: Small-parcel spend audit + UPS/FedEx contract renegotiation on gain-share
product_service: Ingest a shipper's UPS/FedEx/regional-carrier invoice data, benchmark incentives/surcharges, renegotiate the carrier agreement, then audit invoices monthly (billing errors, address-correction/residential surcharges, duplicate charges, the few remaining guaranteed-service refunds). Fee = share of verified savings.
target_customer: Operations/finance lead at e-commerce brands, distributors and light manufacturers with roughly $250k-$5M/yr parcel spend (below the radar of the large negotiation consultancies' sweet spot).
purchase_motivation: Parcel is a top-3 cost line for shippers; annual carrier rate increases and surcharges compound; no-savings-no-fee lowers buyer risk.
spending_evidence: Parcel consultants widely charge only a percentage of savings generated [D, WS14-S020]; an operator since at least 2006 bills a share of actual monthly savings [D, WS14-S019]. Late-delivery refund pool has shrunk: UPS restored guarantees only for next-day air in 2021 [C, WS14-S016]; FedEx keeps most services suspended [A, WS14-S018]; ground services carry no guarantee as of late 2026 [D, WS14-S017].
representative_operators: Refund Retriever, LLC - parcel audit & negotiation since >=2006, fee = share of monthly savings; size unknown [D, WS14-S019]
TransImpact - parcel negotiation/analytics firm marketing percentage-of-savings model [D, WS14-S020]
revenue_mechanism: Percentage of realized savings vs. a contractually defined baseline for the term of the carrier agreement (typically 1-3 yrs), plus % of audit refunds. Exact market fee % MISSING (analyst expectation 25-50% of savings) [E].
typical_transaction_value: Illustrative: $1M/yr parcel spend x 10-20% savings = $100-200k/yr; at an assumed 30% share = $30-60k/yr per client for 2-3 yrs [E].
direct_costs: Analyst time for data normalization and monthly audit; rate-modeling software/data; sales commissions.
contribution_profit_note: Per client perhaps $20-45k/yr contribution after analyst time at assumed fee levels [E].
working_capital_note: No inventory. Savings realized only after new agreement goes live (6-8 week negotiation per WS14-S019) and fees billed monthly/quarterly in arrears; 3-5 months of founder time unpaid before first fee.
sales_cycle: 1-4 months: free benchmark analysis -> signed savings-share agreement -> carrier negotiation (6-8 weeks).
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: savings share over agreement term; renegotiation every 2-3 yrs; ongoing monthly audit.
acquisition_channels: Outbound to e-commerce ops/finance (Shopify/Amazon brand lists, Inc. 5000 lists)
Partnerships with fractional CFOs/bookkeepers and e-commerce agencies
Content: carrier-surcharge teardown posts and free savings calculators
customer_accessibility: Many identifiable shippers; decision-makers reachable by outbound. Credibility wall: buyers are pitched constantly by parcel consultants and must share invoice data.
supplier_accessibility: N/A (no suppliers); carrier account reps must accept negotiation - some carriers push back on third-party consultants [E].
competitive_intensity: high - many parcel consultancies, SaaS audit tools, 3PLs offering pooled rates, carriers' own reps.
entry_strategy: Focus on the $250k-$3M shipper segment with a fast, free, data-driven benchmark and month-to-month audit; specialize in one vertical (e.g., supplements, auto parts) to build benchmark depth.
licenses: None specific; general business registration. Not freight brokerage (no FMCSA authority needed because no transportation is arranged) [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low. Carrier agreements may contain confidentiality clauses restricting disclosure of pricing to third parties [E].
operational_risks: Thin benchmark data vs. incumbents with thousands of agreements; baseline/attribution disputes; data access depends on client exporting carrier billing files.
financial_risks: Clients churn after first renegotiation or migrate to 3PL pooled rates; shipping volume declines cut fees.
founder_expertise: Carrier pricing mechanics (zones, DIM, incentive tiers, accessorials, surcharges), contract structures, negotiation tactics; data analysis fits founder background.
staffing: Founder solo for first ~8-10 clients; then pricing analyst(s) and one sales/BDR.
automation_potential: High: invoice parsing, surcharge anomaly detection, rate modeling, benchmark scenarios can be software/AI-driven at ordinary cost. Negotiation, trust-building and carrier relationship stay human.
delegation_potential: Analysts can run audits with SOPs; negotiation delegable after 2-3 yrs of playbook building.
scalability: National market, but scale limited by sales capacity and benchmark depth; a $1-3M revenue boutique is plausible.
expansion: LTL/TL freight audit (WS14-002), regional-carrier rate brokering, packaging/DIM optimization consulting, 3PL selection advisory.
roic_note: Capital at risk is mostly founder time plus <$12k; ROIC very high if 10+ clients are signed, near zero if not.
critical_assumptions: Sub-$3M shippers still achieve 10-20% savings from renegotiation
A 25-50% savings share is accepted by this segment
unanswered_questions: Published fee % benchmarks for parcel negotiation consultants
Carrier policies toward consultants and confidentiality clauses
Share of SMB shippers already on 3PL/aggregator rates
Typical client retention after first agreement
failure_modes: Cannot beat incumbents' benchmark data, so savings are small
Clients take the new agreement and terminate before savings share accrues

title: Authorized wholesale reseller of established brands on Amazon/Walmart Marketplace
product_service: Buys branded consumer goods at wholesale from brands or their distributors (with written authorization) and resells them on Amazon (FBA) and Walmart Marketplace.
target_customer: Marketplace shoppers buying known brands; supply-side 'customers' are brands needing marketplace coverage.
purchase_motivation: Shoppers want the known brand delivered fast; brands want availability without managing marketplaces themselves.
spending_evidence: Large marketplace demand for branded goods; Amazon referral fees 8-17% by category [B, WS06-S002]. No audited small-reseller economics retrieved.
representative_operators: Numerous small 'Amazon wholesale' sellers; economics self-reported in forums/courses [D]
Pattern Group as the scaled version of buying from brands and reselling (see WS06-003) [C, WS06-S010]
revenue_mechanism: Buy at wholesale (often ~50% of MSRP, assumed) and resell near MAP; margin = spread minus Amazon referral and FBA fees.
typical_transaction_value: $20-$60 per order [E]; wholesale POs $2k-$20k per brand [E]
direct_costs: Wholesale product cost (~45-55% of MSRP, assumed), inbound freight, Amazon referral (typically 15%) [B, WS06-S002], FBA fees [B, WS06-S001], storage, prep (Amazon ended US prep services Jan 2026 per third-party reports - unverified).
contribution_profit_note: Typical target per unit: 8-15% net of fees on sale price [E]; Buy Box shared with other authorized sellers caps velocity.
working_capital_note: Brands usually require prepayment for first orders, net-30 later; inventory turns 4-8x/yr if chosen well [E]; Amazon pays ~biweekly.
sales_cycle: Brand authorization outreach takes 2-12 weeks per brand; many decline.
repeat_purchase: consumable-replenishment if focused on consumable brands (grocery, HPC, pet); otherwise occasional
acquisition_channels: Outbound to brands at trade shows/directories
customer_accessibility: End customers come via Amazon; the real sales job is persuading brands to authorize you.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: many small/mid brands sell to resellers; top brands restrict or sell 1P to Amazon.
competitive_intensity: high - many sellers chase the same open brands; Buy Box rotation compresses margin
entry_strategy: Target small/mid brands with poor Amazon presence and MAP problems; offer listing cleanup and MAP-compliant pricing in exchange for authorization.
licenses: Illinois registration (MyTax Illinois) and resale exemption for purchases [A, WS06-S034]; category gating on Amazon for some brands.
regulatory_barriers: Low; IP/authenticity complaints if sourcing is not documented.
operational_risks: Amazon selling 1P against you, brand revoking authorization, Buy Box loss, suspensions for 'inauthentic' claims.
financial_risks: Thin margins mean a fee change or price war erases profit; slow-moving inventory.
founder_expertise: Amazon operations, brand negotiation, inventory analytics.
staffing: VA for listings/repricing; warehouse/prep help or 3PL.
automation_potential: Repricing, sales-velocity forecasting, brand prospect research and outreach drafting; negotiation stays human.
delegation_potential: Moderate-high; standardized buying rules can be delegated.
scalability: Revenue scales with capital and brand count but margin stays thin; capital-hungry.
expansion: Upgrade to exclusive brand partnerships (WS06-003); add Walmart/Target Plus.
roic_note: 10% net margin x 5 turns = ~50% annual return on inventory [E]; real-world reduced by dead stock.
critical_assumptions: Buy Box share sufficient to turn inventory 4x+
unanswered_questions: Typical authorized-reseller net margins in 2026 (no credible survey retrieved)
Share of brands that restrict marketplace sellers

title: DOT drug & alcohol testing consortium / C-TPA for owner-operators and small fleets
subindustry: DOT consortium and third-party administrator services
product_service: Random-testing pool membership, pre-employment/post-accident/reasonable-suspicion test coordination via lab/MRO/collection-site network, Clearinghouse reporting on employer's behalf, annual MIS reports, supervisor training; optional DOT-qualified on-site collector.
target_customer: Owner-operators and fleets with CDL drivers; Chicago 8-county area has 17,611 recent-filing carriers with 1-5 power units [A, WS17-S001], plus construction/utility employers of CDL drivers.
purchase_motivation: Federal mandate: random testing at baseline 50% (drugs)/10% (alcohol) of driver positions [A, WS17-S006]; Clearinghouse queries [A, WS17-S005]; one-truck operators cannot randomize themselves alone.
spending_evidence: Mandate verified [A, WS17-S005, WS17-S006]; consortium pricing NOT verified (MISSING).
representative_operators: National online consortiums and C/TPAs (names/prices not verified this session) [E]
Occupational health clinics offering DOT testing [E]
revenue_mechanism: Annual enrollment fee per driver plus per-test fees with markup over lab/MRO/collection costs.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis: $75-$200 per driver per year enrollment plus $50-$90 markup-inclusive per drug test [E - unverified]
direct_costs: Lab fees, MRO review fees, third-party collection-site fees, software, staff time.
contribution_profit_note: Low per-member contribution (est. $50-$120/yr) - needs thousands of members or bundling [E].
working_capital_note: Annual fees collected upfront; lab invoices net 30 - slightly positive cash cycle.
sales_cycle: Days; triggered by new authority, new hire, or audit.
customer_accessibility: Owner-operators are numerous and identifiable, but the product is bought online on price.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: SAMHSA-certified labs, MROs and collection networks sell to C/TPAs; contract terms not verified.
entry_strategy: Do not compete standalone; offer as a bundled component of WS17-001 to raise retention and wallet share.
licenses: No specific Illinois licence identified [E]; must follow 49 CFR Part 40 procedures; collector training if collecting in-house [E].
regulatory_barriers: Procedural complexity (Part 40) and liability for errors; Clearinghouse reporting obligations.
operational_risks: Selection/notification errors invalidate random program; chain-of-custody mistakes.
staffing: One administrator can run a large pool with software.
automation_potential: Random selection, notifications, MIS reporting automated; collections stay physical.
expansion: Pre-employment screening, MVRs, background checks (WS12 cross-stream).
roic_note: Asset-light; profit limited by price competition.
critical_assumptions: Bundling raises retention of WS17-001 clients
unanswered_questions: Wholesale lab/MRO/collection rates available to a new C/TPA

title: Temperature-controlled (reefer) brokerage for Chicago-area food & beverage manufacturers
subindustry: Reefer truckload brokerage, food supply chain
product_service: Brokered reefer truckload (and some LTL reefer) moves for food processors, co-packers, cold-storage operators and distributors; temperature-compliance documentation.
target_customer: Logistics managers at regional food & beverage manufacturers, co-packers and cold-storage warehouses ($10M-$500M revenue).
purchase_motivation: Spoilage risk, retailer delivery windows (OTIF fines), FDA sanitary-transport compliance, seasonal produce surges.
spending_evidence: Reefer spot averaged $3.60/mile in Oct 2026 (+$1.12 YoY) [C, WS07-S013]; Chicago food-manufacturing concentration MISSING (not retrieved).
representative_operators: C.H. Robinson (large reefer/produce franchise; segment size not broken out) [A, WS07-S008]
Many specialized reefer brokers (names/sizes not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Load spread; temperature-controlled loads typically command higher per-load revenue [E].
typical_transaction_value: ~$3,000-$4,000 per long-haul reefer load at Oct-2026 rates [E from WS07-S013 per-mile data]; 10-16% margin [E].
direct_costs: Reefer carrier pay, higher-limit cargo insurance, claims deductibles, factoring.
contribution_profit_note: ~$300-$500 per load gross [E]; one rejected/spoiled load can cost several loads' margin [E].
working_capital_note: Same negative cycle as WS07-001 [A-derived, WS07-S009]; claims can tie up cash for months [E].
sales_cycle: Spot same-day; food shippers run annual RFPs; seasonal (produce) bid cycles.
repeat_purchase: recurring — daily/weekly outbound to retailer DCs
acquisition_channels: Outreach to food manufacturers and co-packers
customer_accessibility: Food manufacturers are identifiable (FDA facility registration not public in detail; trade directories) [E]; credibility wall high due to spoilage risk.
supplier_accessibility: Reefer capacity tighter than van; spot nearly equals contract (spread $0.02/mi) [C, WS07-S013], so carriers have leverage.
competitive_intensity: high — produce/reefer is a classic broker vertical.
entry_strategy: Focus on Chicago food corridor outbound lanes, temperature-monitoring documentation, claims discipline.
licenses: FMCSA property-broker operating authority via Motus (identity proofing; min. 8 business days review) [A, WS07-S002]; OP-1 filing fee reportedly $300 [D, WS07-S005]; $75,000 financial security on BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust limited since 2026-01-16 to cash/ILOC/Treasuries [A, WS07-S001]; BOC-3 process agent filing [A, WS07-S002]; UCR $46 (2026) rising to $55 (2027) [A, WS07-S003, WS07-S004]; contingent cargo + general liability insurance not federally mandated but shippers usually require it [E]; no Illinois property-broker license identified [E, not verified]. FDA Sanitary Transportation rule (21 CFR Part 1 Subpart O) duties may apply to brokers acting as 'shippers' [E, not verified].
regulatory_barriers: Food-safety transport compliance; same FMCSA broker rules.
operational_risks: Temperature excursions, rejected loads, food & beverage is a frequent cargo-theft target [E; CargoNet commodity breakdown not retrieved].
financial_risks: Large claims (whole load value), shipper concentration, contract-rate squeeze when spot≈contract [C, WS07-S013].
geographic_constraints: Chicago-area food cluster gives density; not required.
founder_expertise: Reefer operations (pulp temps, continuous vs cycle, pre-cooling), claims handling, food-safety paperwork.
automation_potential: Telematics temperature feeds, automated exception alerts, quoting.
delegation_potential: Moderate; reefer desk skills are hireable.
scalability: Add reps and lanes; food demand resilient.
expansion: Cold-storage partnerships, LTL reefer consolidation, produce seasonality desks.
roic_note: Similar to WS07-001 with higher claim risk capital buffer [E].
critical_assumptions: Food shippers accept a new broker for backup/spot lanes
unanswered_questions: Chicago-area food manufacturing establishment counts (Census CBP not retrieved)
Typical reefer broker margins vs van (no public split)
failure_modes: Tight reefer capacity forces negative-margin coverage
RFP-dominated buyers never award a newcomer

title: Junk removal and hauling (with optional dumpster rental)
product_service: Full-service removal of household junk, furniture, appliances, estate and renovation debris by a 2-person truck crew; small roll-off/dumpster rentals.
target_customer: Homeowners and renters (moves, cleanouts, estates), realtors, property managers, small contractors.
purchase_motivation: Urgent, labor-saving disposal; moving, estate settlement, renovation.
spending_evidence: Junk King 166 US units averaged $553,959 gross sales in 2024 (median $435,663; bottom quartile $193,696), avg $399/job [B, WS18-S001].
representative_operators: Junk King — 172 US units, avg $554k [B, WS18-S001]
1-800-GOT-JUNK, College Hunks Hauling Junk, JunkLuggers (Item 19 not retrieved)
Many independent owner-operators
revenue_mechanism: Volume-based price per load fraction × jobs; dumpster rental per drop.
direct_costs: Crew labor (20.6% of sales), dump fees (7.2%), fuel (3.3%) per Junk King survey; franchise licence 8% and call-centre 5% avoided by independent [B, WS18-S001].
contribution_profit_note: Junk King franchise gross profit 56.3% after franchise fees, before rent, truck payments, insurance, marketing [B, WS18-S001]; independent ≈65-70% before self-funded marketing and call handling [E].
working_capital_note: Paid at job completion; dump fees same-day; truck purchase/lease is the main capital need.
repeat_purchase: occasional — repeat via realtors/property managers; consumers infrequent.
acquisition_channels: Estate attorneys and senior move managers
customer_accessibility: High — buyers search at moment of need.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed — trucks/trailers available used; transfer stations and recyclers accessible (fees vary by municipality).
competitive_intensity: high — three national franchise brands plus many independents.
entry_strategy: Same-day service, photo/video instant quotes, donation/recycling diversion story, B2B accounts with property managers and realtors.
licenses: No Illinois licence specific to junk removal identified. Whether ICC household goods licence applies to hauling customers' goods for disposal is unclear [A for licence existence, WS18-S014]. Municipal waste-hauler licensing (Chicago/suburbs) MISSING. Commercial auto insurance, GL, workers' comp.
regulatory_barriers: Low; disposal rules for appliances (refrigerant), electronics (Illinois electronics landfill ban — not verified), tires, paint.
operational_risks: Worker injury (lifting), truck downtime, property damage.
financial_risks: Truck capital; marketing costs; seasonality (winter slower).
founder_expertise: Pricing by volume, crew management, digital marketing.
staffing: Founder + 1 helper initially; crews of 2 per truck; dispatcher at 2-3 trucks.
automation_potential: Photo-based quoting, AI phone/text booking, routing. Labor remains manual.
delegation_potential: Good — crew leads and dispatcher are standard roles.
scalability: Moderate: add trucks within metro; top Junk King quartile ~$1.1M [B, WS18-S001].
expansion: Dumpster rental, estate cleanouts, demolition (light), donation pickup partnerships, hoarding cleanouts.
critical_assumptions: Independent can replace franchise call-centre/brand with own marketing at ≤10% of sales
Dump fees in Chicagoland similar to system average 7.2%
unanswered_questions: Customer acquisition cost per job in Chicago
failure_modes: Underpriced loads after dump fees and labor
